h: Penicillin, wireless and a free wander through genius
p: The museum as we know it was founded in 1924, when collector Lewis Evans gave his collection of scientific instruments to the university. That gift is still the core of what you see today, and the astrolabes in particular are among the most important collections of their kind anywhere.

There is a strong Oxford story to discover too. Look out for displays about the development of penicillin, which was turned into a life-saving medicine by a team of scientists in Oxford during the Second World War. Seeing the homemade equipment they used is a powerful reminder of how much changed thanks to a bit of ingenuity and a lot of hard graft.

The museum also has objects linked to Guglielmo Marconi and the early days of wireless, which help explain how radio came about. For older kids into science, it is a cracking way to see how the gadgets they use today have deep roots.
Entry is free, so it is easy to pop in for an hour without guilt.

Afterwards, Broad Street has plenty to explore. Blackwell's bookshop is just across the road and has a famous underground room packed with books. Turn the corner and you will find the Radcliffe Camera and the Bridge of Sighs. The Ashmolean Museum on Beaumont Street and the Pitt Rivers and Natural History Museum on Parks Road are both free too, making Oxford a brilliant city for museum hopping.
